title: SR&ED for Environmental Regulation Compliance | Canada FAQ
description: Can work done to meet environmental regulations qualify for SR&ED tax incentives in Canada? See what the rules say.
summary: This page explains whether work done to meet environmental regulations can qualify for SR&ED tax incentives in Canada. Compliance alone is not enough: under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, routine testing and commercial production are excluded, so Canadian businesses must show technological uncertainty, technological advancement and a systematic investigation supported by contemporaneous documentation.

Compliance alone is not enough: under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, routine testing and commercial production are excluded, so Canadian businesses must show technological uncertainty, technological advancement and a systematic investigation supported by contemporaneous documentation.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada operates one of the most comprehensive and generous research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive regimes among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) jurisdictions, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada, the SR&ED program represents the federal government's single largest fiscal instrument supporting industrial innovation, assisting more than 24,160 businesses annually and disbursing approximately $4.6 billion in investment tax credits (ITCs) across 23,677 processed claims during the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle.

The statutory architecture of the federal regime rests upon a dual-benefit mechanism codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). The first statutory pillar, governed by subsection 37(1) of the ITA, authorizes taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool allowable current and—following recent legislative restoration—qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada. Taxpayers may deduct this cumulative expenditure pool in whole or in part to reduce taxable income in the current taxation year, or carry the unapplied pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. The second statutory pillar, governed by section 127 and specifically defined under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, grants an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage of the claimant's "qualified expenditures" for the taxation year. Depending upon the legal classification, ownership structure, and financial scale of the claimant, the resulting ITC operates either as a fully refundable cash disbursement—providing critical non-dilutive capital to pre-revenue and loss-making innovators—or as a non-refundable tax offset that may be carried back three taxation years and carried forward up to twenty taxation years. When an SR&ED ITC is utilized to offset tax payable or refunded in cash, the amount of the credit is included in the taxpayer's taxable income in the subsequent taxation year (or reduces the section 37 deductible expenditure pool), establishing a self-balancing fiscal mechanism across consecutive reporting periods.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most profound structural transformation since the 2012–2014 federal overhaul. Following two formal rounds of public consultations initiated by the Department of Finance Canada between January 31, 2024, and May 27, 2024, alongside policy announcements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES 2024) and Budget 2025, Parliament enacted the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (Bill C-15), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (and for capital property acquired after December 15, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the expenditure limit for the enhanced 35 per cent refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million, expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35 per cent refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, and reinstated the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and shared-use equipment (SUE). Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA operationalized an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process delivering upfront eligibility determinations within eight weeks prior to project commencement, while the Province of Québec replaced seven legacy innovation tax measures with the unified Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.

body.text: Federal SR&ED Legislative Framework and the Bill C-15 Reforms
Evolution of Policy from the 2024 Consultations to Royal Assent of Bill C-15

The legislative modernization culminating in Bill C-15 originated from structural pressures in Canada's innovation economy, specifically declining business enterprise R&D (BERD) intensity, capital flight of domestic intellectual property (IP), and the real-value erosion of the $3 million expenditure limit due to cumulative wage inflation across scientific and engineering disciplines. On January 31, 2024, the Department of Finance Canada initiated Phase One of its formal public consultation on the SR&ED program, soliciting stakeholder submissions through April 15, 2024, across seven foundational policy questions: maintaining program effectiveness in supporting R&D investment across businesses of all types, better supporting the growth and scale-up of R&D-intensive Canadian enterprises, modernizing the statutory definition of SR&ED and its eligibility criteria, improving complementarity with Canada's suite of direct R&D support programs, targeting overall assistance more effectively within cost-neutral parameters, ensuring the domestic retention of intellectual property so innovative firms remain Canadian-owned and operated, and streamlining administrative compliance for entrepreneurs. Following the presentation of Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) in the House of Commons by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance on April 16, 2024, a second phase of SR&ED consultations ran through May 27, 2024.

While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed an intermediate increase of the enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million alongside an expanded phase-out range, Budget 2025 superseded that interim proposal by establishing a $6 million annual expenditure cap. These legislative enhancements were consolidated into the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (Bill C-15), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Looking forward, Budget 2026 announced the federal government's intention to initiate further consultations on additional SR&ED structural reforms, while also incorporating intellectual property protection costs and advancing proposals for a broader Productivity Mega Deduction to stimulate capital formation.
Detailed Mechanics of the Enhanced 35% and Basic 15% Investment Tax Credits

The federal SR&ED program operates on a two-tier volume-based credit rate structure rather than an incremental or sliding-scale rate. Under section 127 of the ITA, the applicable credit percentage and refundability profile depend upon the corporate classification of the taxpayer and the quantum of qualified expenditures incurred during the taxation year.

Under the enhanced 35 per cent refundable tier, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an enhanced 35 per cent ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs, the 35 per cent ITC earned on qualifying current expenditures is 100 per cent refundable under section 127.1 of the ITA, generating up to $2,100,000 in annual cash refunds regardless of whether the corporation has federal income tax payable. This doubles the previous maximum annual refundable cash ceiling of $1,050,000 that applied under the pre-Bill C-15 $3,000,000 expenditure limit.

Under the basic 15 per cent non-refundable tier, qualified expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC in excess of its $6,000,000 expenditure limit (or its reduced expenditure limit following phase-out) earn the basic 15 per cent ITC. The basic 15 per cent rate also applies to all qualified expenditures of corporations that do not qualify as CCPCs or ECPCs—most notably Canadian subsidiaries controlled directly or indirectly by foreign multinational enterprises, as well as public corporations failing the ECPC criteria. For corporations subject to the 15 per cent rate, the credit is non-refundable and may only be applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, with unused credit balances eligible for a three-year carryback and a twenty-year carryforward.

For unincorporated entities, trusts, and partnerships, distinct flow-through and refundability rules govern credit utilization. Individuals (sole proprietorships) and trusts carrying on business in Canada earn the basic 15 per cent ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures. Because a partnership is not a separate taxable person under the ITA, it cannot claim an SR&ED ITC in its own right; instead, the partnership's SR&ED expenditures and resulting credits flow through and are allocated to its members at the partner level. Because credits allocated to individual partners are generally non-refundable, unincorporated founders conducting substantial R&D face a strong fiscal incentive to incorporate as a CCPC or ECPC prior to incurring project costs.
Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue Elections

To target refundable fiscal support toward small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and domestic mid-market scale-ups, the $6,000,000 baseline expenditure limit is shared across an associated corporate group (allocated via Schedule T2SCH49) and is subject to a statutory phase-out. Under Bill C-15, for taxation years starting after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital phase-out band was expanded from its historical $10 million–$50 million range to a new threshold starting at $15,000,000 and fully eliminating at $75,000,000, representing a $60,000,000 linear reduction range under updated subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA.

Under the pre-Bill C-15 rules (and subsequent to the earlier repeal of the federal taxable income phase-out test), the historical federal formula phased out the $3,000,000 limit linearly as prior-year taxable capital rose from $10,000,000 to $50,000,000.

Beyond expanding the taxable capital thresholds, Bill C-15 introduced two structural innovations to the phase-out architecture that alter corporate financing incentives in Canada. First, Bill C-15 extended access to the enhanced 35 per cent refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), defined as corporations resident in Canada that have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or that have elected or been designated to be a public corporation) and are not controlled directly or indirectly by non-residents. Historically, a Canadian technology or life-sciences CCPC that executed an initial public offering (IPO) on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or TSX Venture Exchange immediately lost its CCPC status, forfeiting the 35 per cent refundable credit and dropping to the 15 per cent non-refundable tier. Under Bill C-15, domestic public innovators retain access to the $6,000,000 enhanced refundable limit, with their expenditure limit phased out using a three-year average gross revenue test rather than taxable capital. Second, Bill C-15 permits CCPCs and their associated groups—particularly capital-intensive clean-technology, biotechnology, and hardware scale-ups whose balance-sheet taxable capital exceeds $15 million due to equity or debt financings despite low commercial revenue—to formally elect to have their $6,000,000 expenditure limit phase-out calculated using the revenue-based phase-out thresholds applicable to ECPCs instead of taxable capital.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Complementary CCA Immediate Expensing

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (depreciable property) and capital lease payments were statutorily excluded from both the section 37 SR&ED deduction pool and the section 127 ITC calculation. Recognizing that modern artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), semiconductor, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing R&D requires substantial capital infrastructure—such as graphics processing unit (GPU) compute clusters, specialized laboratory apparatus, and pilot-scale fabrication tools—Bill C-15 restored the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) for property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024.

Under the restored capital rules reflected on updated Form T661 (26), claimants may include 100 per cent of allowable capital expenditures for depreciable property used all or substantially all (90 per cent or more of its operating time over its useful life) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, as well as partial capital claims under the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy for new equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that is used primarily in SR&ED. Furthermore, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, are once again eligible, provided the underlying capital expenditure for the leased equipment was made by the performer/lessor after December 15, 2024. Expenditures for depreciable property or for the right to use property acquired before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives. When a claimant elects to use the traditional overhead method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90 per cent of the time are claimed on Line 360 of Form T661 (26) as overhead and other expenditures.

For capital assets that do not meet the strict SR&ED usage thresholds or are deployed in broader commercial digital transformation, Bill C-15 and Budget 2024 enacted complementary Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) and Clean Economy measures. First, Bill C-15 provides immediate 100 per cent first-year expensing for qualifying purchases of property acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027, across three targeted productivity asset classes: Class 44 (patents or rights to use patented information), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment and systems software). Second, Bill C-15 temporarily reinstates the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII) and immediate expensing for qualifying depreciable assets acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030, providing an enhanced first-year CCA deduction before phasing out between 2030 and 2033 (whereas under prior rules the AII was being phased out between 2024 and 2027). Third, alongside Bill C-59 and Budget 2024, the federal government deployed five refundable Clean Economy ITCs: the Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) ITC, the Clean Technology ITC, the Clean Hydrogen ITC, the Clean Electricity ITC (available where provincial and territorial Crown corporations commit to a net-zero electricity grid by 2035 and pass credit value through to ratepayers), and the 30 per cent Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC. The 30 per cent Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC covers investments in eligible property used all or substantially all to manufacture clean technology or to carry out qualifying mineral activities (extraction, processing at mine or well sites, tailing ponds, mills, smelters, or refineries, recycling, and graphite activities) producing copper, nickel, cobalt, lithium, graphite, and rare earth elements. Effective for property acquired on or after January 1, 2024, Budget 2024 modified the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC to accommodate polymetallic projects by allowing property used in qualifying mineral activities expected to produce primarily (50 per cent or more of the financial value of output) qualifying materials at mine or well sites, supported by an arm's-length engineer or geoscientist attestation and a five-year average historical price safe-harbour rule against recapture.
Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Judicial Precedents
Analysis of Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to both federal and provincial R&D tax relief in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which conforms generally to the OECD Frascati Manual and restricts eligibility to the natural sciences and engineering. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and divides qualifying technical work into four distinct statutory branches.

The first branch, basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a), encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. In practice, basic research accounts for the smallest proportion of corporate SR&ED claims, occurring predominantly within universities and specialized research institutes. The second branch, applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b), covers work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and largest corporate branch, experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The fourth branch, eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d), permits claimants to include work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but strictly to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c).

Conversely, subsection 248(1) excludes commercial and routine engineering activities from the definition of SR&ED, including market research or sales promotion, quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes, research in the social sciences or the humanities, mineral or petroleum prospecting, exploration, drilling, or production, commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or commercial use of a new or improved process, style changes, and routine data collection. Where experimental development occurs on an industrial plant floor alongside commercial production runs, the CRA's Production Runs Policy distinguishes between an Experimental Development + Experimental Production (ED+EP) context and the default Experimental Development + Commercial Production (ED+CP) context, ensuring that only the incremental expenditures necessitated by the experimental phase enter the SR&ED claim.
The Five-Question Judicial Standard and the CRA Three-Test Framework

Canadian jurisprudence governing the technical eligibility of SR&ED claims is anchored in the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC). At paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman established five cumulative criteria that Canadian courts and the CRA apply to determine whether a project constitutes SR&ED. In its administrative policies and Guide T4088, the CRA synthesizes the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria into a Three-Test Eligibility Framework that every claimed project must satisfy.

First, under the Scientific or Technological Uncertainty test, the claimant must demonstrate that a technological risk or uncertainty existed that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard practice. Technological uncertainty arises when the probability of achieving a given technical objective or system constraint cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of publicly available scientific knowledge, standard engineering principles, or the established practice of competent professionals in the field. Mere commercial uncertainty, project complexity, or a claimant's internal lack of familiarity with existing off-the-shelf software or engineering techniques does not constitute technological uncertainty.

Second, under the Scientific or Technological Advancement test, the investigation must be undertaken to generate new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the understanding of underlying scientific relations or technological capabilities. Crucially, whether a project succeeds commercially or technically is irrelevant to SR&ED eligibility: a failed experimental project that systematically proves why a hypothesized technical architecture cannot work generates valid new technological knowledge and fully qualifies for the credit.

Third, under the Systematic Investigation or Search test, the claimant must show that the work proceeded via the scientific method—formulating specific hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty, testing those hypotheses through structured experiment or analysis, observing and evaluating quantifiable results, and drawing logical conclusions as the work progressed. To substantiate this systematic progression during a CRA review, claimants must maintain contemporaneous documentation—records created during the actual performance of the R&D (such as dated test logs, code repositories, engineering benches, and failure analyses) rather than narratives reconstructed retroactively at tax-filing time.
Analysis of Key Tax Court of Canada Precedents

The application of the Northwest Hydraulic framework has been reinforced through a consistent body of Tax Court of Canada (TCC) jurisprudence that governs CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) audit determinations. In Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC (2014-1594(IT)I), the Tax Court reaffirmed that the legal burden of proof rests squarely upon the taxpayer to establish, through verifiable contemporaneous evidence rather than conclusory assertions, that each of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria has been met.

Subsequently, in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, the Tax Court dismissed the taxpayer's appeal and clarified the strict boundary under Question 2 of Northwest Hydraulic between genuine technological uncertainty and bespoke custom engineering. The Court held that designing complex, custom-engineered theatrical rigging equipment by applying established mechanical engineering principles and iterative trial-and-error adjustments—without formulating and testing scientific hypotheses to overcome a fundamental limitation in underlying engineering knowledge—constitutes routine engineering rather than SR&ED. Conversely, in Canafric Inc. v. The King, the Tax Court upheld the taxpayer's SR&ED tax credits, confirming that where existing food-science and process parameters cannot predict the behaviour of novel formulations and the claimant conducts systematic, documented experimentation to resolve that technological uncertainty in accordance with the standard interpreted in Joel Theatrical Rigging, the expenditures qualify for SR&ED relief.

body.text: Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Calculation Methods, and Statutory Restrictions
The Traditional Method vs. The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method

Once a project satisfies the technical eligibility threshold under subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its allowable SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) and its "qualified expenditures" for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations. A claimant must elect annually on Form T661—across all projects for the taxation year—to calculate its SR&ED expenditures using either the Traditional Method (ITA clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)) or the Proxy Method (ITA subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI)).

Under the Proxy Method, instead of specifically tracking and allocating indirect overhead and support expenditures, the claimant calculates a notional amount known as the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations. Since the 2014 calendar year (following staged reductions from 65 per cent for 2012 and prior years and 60 per cent for 2013, prorated for taxation years straddling January 1, 2014), the PPA is calculated at a flat rate of 55 per cent of the claimant's eligible "salary base" (reported on Line 820 in Part 5, Section B of Form T661), subject to the overall cap on the PPA governed by subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations. The salary base consists solely of the portion of salaries and wages of employees who are directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (including directly engaged salary or wages for SR&ED undertaken in other countries only to the extent governed by subsection 2900(5) ASA salary rules, though domestic SR&ED forms the standard base). Crucially, while the 55 per cent PPA is included in "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) to earn the federal (and applicable provincial) ITC, the PPA is a purely notional figure and cannot be included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA remain deductible as ordinary business expenses in computing income under subsection 9(1) of the ITA. Furthermore, a retiring allowance cannot be claimed under the proxy method because retiring allowances are statutorily deemed to be encompassed within the PPA.

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the 55 per cent PPA and instead specifically identifies, tracks, allocates, and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures under subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Regulations. These encompass salaries or wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the performance of SR&ED (other than those directly engaged), expenditures directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED under paragraph 2900(2)(c) (including eligible SR&ED training costs), and expenditures directly attributable or directly related and incremental to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED under subsection 2900(3) and paragraph 2900(3)(b) (including post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs where SR&ED usage is less than 90 per cent, claimed on Line 360 of Form T661). Actual overhead and other expenditures substantiated under the traditional method are both added to the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and included in qualified expenditures for ITC calculation. While most Canadian claimants elect the proxy method due to its administrative simplicity and generous 55 per cent notional uplift, capital-intensive or facility-heavy operations whose actual incremental SR&ED overhead exceeds 55 per cent of directly engaged wages should model both methods prior to filing.

body.text: Detailed Eligibility Rules for Specific Expenditure Categories
Salaries and Wages and the "Directly Engaged" Standard

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is determined strictly by the hands-on technical tasks performed by the individual rather than by the employee's corporate job title. Direct engagement refers to hands-on scientific or experimental work, including preparing equipment and materials for experiments, operating experimental prototypes, writing and testing experimental source code, collecting and analysing experimental data, and providing direct technical supervision to personnel performing hands-on SR&ED. Every dollar of salary claimed must be linked to a specific eligible project, a specific employee, and contemporaneous time records.
Restrictions on Specified Employees (Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9))

Stringent anti-avoidance rules govern the salaries and wages of a "specified employee", defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as an employee who is a specified shareholder of the employer (generally owning, directly or indirectly, 10 per cent or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or any related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. Under section 6.0 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and subsection 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations, specified employees are barred from including bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable employment benefits under paragraph 6(1)(a) of the ITA, excess employee profit-sharing plan (EPSP) allocations subject to special tax under subsection 207.8(2) (where employer EPSP contributions allocated to a specified employee exceed 20 per cent of the employee's total other employment income received in the year, rendering the excess non-deductible under paragraph 8(1)(o.2)), or unpaid salary or wages from a prior taxation year that are paid in the current year. Furthermore, directly engaged SR&ED wages claimed for a specified employee cannot exceed 75 per cent of that employee's total salary or wages (excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages).

For purposes of computing the 55 per cent PPA salary base under subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations, the maximum amount that a claimant can include in the salary base for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of two statutory ceilings. The first ceiling is 75 per cent of the specified employee's total salary or wages across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties (excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid salary or wages paid in the year). The second ceiling is 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, prorated for the number of days of employment in the taxation year:

where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual. Statutory rules specify that there is no proration for the portion of the year during which the employee was not yet a specified employee. If a specified employee is also employed by one or more associated corporations during the taxation year, subsection 2900(8) of the Regulations restricts the aggregate proxy salary base across the associated corporate group to the single prorated 2.5 × YMPE limit.
Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA, claimants may include 100 per cent of the cost of materials consumed (rendered virtually worthless or destroyed during the course of experimentation) or materials transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test rig during SR&ED). However, if transformed materials or experimental property are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, SR&ED recapture provisions apply to claw back the associated ITC and increase tax otherwise payable.
Subcontractors, Taxable Suppliers, and Third-Party Payments (80% Rule)

When a claimant contracts out eligible basic research, applied research, experimental development, or directly supporting work to an arm's-length contractor to be performed on the claimant's behalf, 100 per cent of the contract expenditure is deductible in the subsection 37(1) pool, but only 80 per cent of the contract expenditure is included in "qualified expenditures" for ITC calculation under subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Two strict statutory conditions govern subcontractor eligibility. First, the contracted SR&ED work must be physically carried out in Canada; payments for R&D performed outside Canada earn zero investment tax credit. Second, under the CRA's Total Qualified Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (Section 9.0) and subsection 127(9), a current SR&ED contract expenditure paid or payable to or for the benefit of a person or partnership is excluded from qualified expenditures unless that contractor is a taxable supplier (generally a Canadian resident taxpayer or a Canadian permanent establishment of a non-resident subject to Canadian income tax).

Similarly, 80 per cent of third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D consortia qualify for the ITC under subsection 127(9), provided the SR&ED is carried out in Canada, relates to a business of the claimant, and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of that SR&ED.
Prescribed Expenditures, Unpaid Amounts, and the Government Assistance Grind

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA and section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations (detailed in Section 10.0 of the Total Qualified Expenditures Policy), "prescribed expenditures" are excluded from qualified expenditures. Most notably, SR&ED claim-preparation fees (such as professional accounting, legal, or contingency-fee consulting charges incurred to prepare Form T661) are prescribed expenditures that must be subtracted in arriving at total qualified expenditures; while deductible as ordinary business expenses under subsection 9(1), they do not earn the SR&ED ITC. Furthermore, unpaid expenditures that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which they were incurred are excluded from qualified expenditures for that year; when an unpaid contract expenditure is subsequently paid in a later taxation year, only 80 per cent of the amount paid is added to qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year of payment.

Finally, under subsection 127(9), a claimant's qualified expenditures must be reduced ("ground down") by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (reported on Line 513 of Form T661) as well as direct federal and provincial innovation grants constitute government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base dollar-for-dollar. Similarly, where a business performs SR&ED on behalf of another party on a contract basis (or receives a contract payment for SR&ED, excluding joint or collaborative R&D arrangements), it must reduce its qualified expenditures to prevent double-claiming of the same R&D work by both the payer and the performer. Conversely, if a claimant repays government assistance or a contract payment in a subsequent year that previously reduced its qualified expenditures, the repayment is added back to the expenditure pool on Line 560 of Form T661.
Federal Administration, Pre-Claim Approval, and Statutory Filing Procedures
Required Tax Forms and Compliance Documentation

Claiming federal SR&ED incentives requires the synchronous preparation of prescribed technical and financial schedules filed alongside the annual corporate or personal income tax return. The primary technical and financial claim form is Form T661 (26), Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, which was updated by the CRA in 2026 to incorporate all legislative changes enacted under Bill C-15, supported by Guide T4088, Guide to Form T661. Part 2 of Form T661 captures project-by-project technical descriptions addressing the three core eligibility tests (scientific or technological advancement, technological uncertainty, and systematic investigation supported by contemporaneous documentation). Parts 3 and 4 quantify allowable current and restored capital SR&ED expenditures, including Line 360 for post-December 15, 2024 equipment lease costs where SR&ED usage is under 90 per cent under the traditional method, Line 513 for provincial government assistance, Line 557 for total current SR&ED expenditures (used for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024), Line 559 for total qualified SR&ED expenditures, and Line 560 for repayments of government assistance or contract payments. Part 5, Section B calculates the directly engaged salary base and the 55 per cent Prescribed Proxy Amount on Line 820.

Alongside Form T661, corporations must file Schedule T2SCH31 (Schedule 31), Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, with their T2 Corporation Income Tax Return to calculate the 35 per cent or 15 per cent ITC, apply the $6 million expenditure limit, and claim current-year cash refunds, tax offsets, or three-year carrybacks and twenty-year carryforwards. Where a CCPC or ECPC is associated with one or more corporations in the taxation year, the group must also file Schedule T2SCH49 (Schedule 49), Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit, to allocate the shared $6 million expenditure limit. Note also that in its recent administrative updates, the CRA formally archived its historical guidance document Guidelines for SR&ED claims made by physicians and medical professional corporations – Information for claimants, directing medical claimants to rely on the core consolidated SR&ED policies.
The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

While a Canadian corporation's T2 income tax return is due within six months of its fiscal year-end (and any balance of corporate taxes owed is generally due two months after fiscal year-end), subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA establish a specific reporting window for SR&ED claims: a corporation has 12 months after its T2 filing due date—which equals 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred—to file a completed Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31. For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 fiscal year-end has a T2 filing due date of June 30, 2025, and faces a firm SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2026. Set out in the CRA's Filing Requirements Policy, this 18-month deadline is a strict statutory bar with no extensions or late-filing relief: if a claimant fails to file Form T661 and Schedule 31 containing the prescribed project and expenditure details within 18 months of fiscal year-end, the SR&ED deduction and ITC entitlement for that taxation year are permanently extinguished.
The CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

Historically, the SR&ED program operated exclusively on a retrospective post-filing audit model, leaving businesses uncertain whether the CRA would accept the technical eligibility of their R&D projects until months after the fiscal year concluded and capital had already been expended. To eliminate this predictability gap, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its new optional Pre-Claim Approval Process. Through a streamlined digital application submitted via the CRA's My Business Account portal before the business begins R&D work or incurs project costs, eligible claimants can obtain a formal pre-claim approval determination from the CRA within eight weeks. This eight-week pre-claim determination confirms upfront whether the proposed project qualifies for SR&ED tax incentives, enabling corporate leadership to plan R&D budgets and capital investments with regulatory certainty.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon Territory operates a dedicated R&D tax credit that layers atop the federal SR&ED ITC for corporations that maintain a permanent establishment and physically conduct eligible R&D within that province or territory. Except for Québec (administered independently by Revenu Québec via the CO-17 corporate return) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration via the AT1 corporate return), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered centrally by the CRA through supplemental schedules filed with the federal T2 return.

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of Major Provincial Regimes
Ontario: The Dual OITC and ORDTC Regime and Stacking Mechanics
Ontario operates two distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sch. A, that interact sequentially with one another and with the federal SR&ED ITC.

The Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), governed by section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and Ontario Regulation 37/09 and claimed on T2 Schedule 566, provides an 8 per cent fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10 per cent for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016) to qualifying corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures, yielding a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000 (down from $300,000 prior to June 1, 2016). Critically, Ontario's $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is an independent provincial statutory threshold and did not increase when federal Bill C-15 doubled the federal expenditure limit to $6,000,000; consequently, an Ontario CCPC incurring $6,000,000 of qualifying Ontario R&D expenditures earns the 8 per cent OITC on its first $3,000,000 of spend, and only the federal 35 per cent ITC (plus the 3.5 per cent non-refundable ORDTC) on the tranche between $3,000,000 and $6,000,000. Furthermore, the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations, prorated for short taxation years based on the number of days in proportion to 365, and phased out linearly if the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income lies between $500,000 and $800,000 or if its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. When a corporation falls inside both phase-out ranges simultaneously, the two survival ratios multiply rather than taking the lesser of the two: for instance, a corporation with $700,000 of prior-year taxable income (retaining one-third, or $1,000,000, of the $3,000,000 limit) and $30,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital (retaining four-fifths of the capital band) sees its OITC expenditure limit reduced to $800,000 ($3,000,000 × 1/3 × 4/5), yielding a maximum OITC of $64,000. Following the enactment of federal Bill C-15, Ontario updated its qualified expenditure rules to include 100 per cent of current expenditures and 100 per cent of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures made between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, remain excluded, and capital expenditures made before January 1, 2014, were included at 40 per cent). Note that while the 2018 Ontario Budget proposed an enhanced 12 per cent OITC rate for firms with an Ontario R&D-to-gross-revenue ratio of 20 per cent or above (subject to maintaining at least 90 per cent of prior-year R&D spend), that proposal was never enacted into law, leaving the statutory OITC rate at a flat 8 per cent.

The Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on T2 Schedule 508 (with worksheet S580WS), provides a 3.5 per cent non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5 per cent for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) available to all corporations (CCPCs, public corporations, and foreign-controlled subsidiaries) with a permanent establishment in Ontario. The ORDTC has no expenditure cap, and unused credits may be carried back 3 years or carried forward 20 years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. For multinational R&D centres operating in Ontario, the 3.5 per cent ORDTC represents a substantial recovery (for example, $700,000 annually on a $20,000,000 R&D budget) that must be incorporated into inter-company transfer pricing agreements and deferred tax asset valuations.

In computing combined federal-Ontario recovery, Ontario law explicitly designates the 8 per cent OITC as government assistance that reduces the eligible expenditure pool for the 3.5 per cent ORDTC, while both the OITC and the ORDTC constitute provincial government assistance that reduces the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base on Line 513 of Form T661. Consequently, for a qualifying Ontario CCPC incurring $1,000,000 of eligible current SR&ED expenditures in Ontario (with prior-year taxable income of $300,000 and prior-year taxable capital of $5,000,000, well below the $500,000 and $25,000,000 phase-out thresholds, and with no other grants), the exact three-step calculation proceeds as follows: first, the corporation calculates its 8 per cent OITC on the full $1,000,000 of eligible Ontario expenditures, yielding $80,000 of refundable credit; second, it calculates the 3.5 per cent ORDTC on the expenditure pool net of the OITC ($1,000,000 − $80,000 = $920,000), yielding $32,200 of non-refundable credit; and third, it reduces its federal qualified expenditures by both provincial credits ($1,000,000 − $80,000 − $32,200 = $887,800) and applies the 35 per cent federal ITC, yielding $310,730 of refundable federal credit. Combining the three steps ($80,000 + $32,200 + $310,730) produces a total combined tax credit recovery of $422,930 (an effective recovery rate of 42.29 per cent on $1,000,000 of spend, comprising $390,730 [39.07%] in immediate refundable cash and $32,200 [3.22%] in non-refundable Ontario tax credits). Note that if a CCPC has no foreseeable Ontario corporate income tax liability, it may elect to renounce the 3.5 per cent ORDTC so that the $32,200 non-refundable credit does not grind down its 35 per cent refundable federal ITC.
Québec: The CRIC Overhaul (Effective for Tax Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

In its 2025–2026 Budget, the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive overhaul of its provincial innovation tax regime administered by Revenu Québec. For taxation years of corporations (and fiscal periods of partnerships) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished seven legacy R&D and innovation tax incentives: first, the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly claimed on Form RD-1029.7-V with associated corporation agreement Form RD-1029.7.8-T); second, the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6-V); third, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V); fourth, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V, subject to a transitional carryforward rule allowing a taxpayer or partnership with an eligible fee balance at the end of a tax year or fiscal period ending after March 25, 2025, to claim the consortium credit under legacy terms for tax years ending on or before December 31, 2029); fifth, the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; sixth, the industrial design component of the in-house design tax credits (while leaving the fashion design component intact); and seventh, the personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. R&D tax credit eligibility on the individual income tax return (TP-1) was also eliminated.

Replacing those seven legacy measures for taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, is the new Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), which can only be claimed by qualified corporations and corporations that are members of a qualified partnership carrying on business and maintaining an establishment in Québec. Unlike the federal SR&ED program—which terminates eligibility the moment technological uncertainty is resolved—the CRIC supports both core scientific R&D and downstream pre-commercialization activities (such as product certification, regulatory compliance testing, industrial design, and pre-commercial prototyping tied to an R&D initiative in Québec). Eligible CRIC expenditures encompass 100 per cent of salaries and wages for R&D and pre-commercialization personnel in Québec, 100 per cent of capital expenditures (CAPEX) for depreciable equipment acquired for R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec (subject to exclusions for property used in a large investment project benefiting from a tax holiday), and 50 per cent of consideration paid to subcontractors and eligible public research organizations (such as universities, College Centres for the Transfer of Technology [CCTTs], and eligible public research centres or research consortia, for which the Minister of the Economy, Innovation and Energy continues to issue qualification certificates under the Act respecting the sectoral parameters of certain fiscal measures).

The CRIC is 100 per cent refundable for all qualifying corporations (including CCPCs, public corporations, and foreign-owned subsidiaries operating in Québec) and operates on a two-bracket spending schedule. The corporation earns a 30 per cent refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible CRIC expenditures above the annual exclusion threshold (shared among associated corporations), and a 20 per cent refundable rate on all eligible CRIC expenditures exceeding $1,000,000, with no upper expenditure ceiling. Where a corporation claims the CRIC as a member of a qualified partnership, the applicable credit rate is a flat 20 per cent (reported using codes 112 and 113 on lines 440p to 440y of the CO-17 corporate return per Revenu Québec Guide CO-17.G). Before applying the 30 per cent or 20 per cent CRIC rates, total eligible expenses for the taxation year must exceed a modified annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold (calculated as a base amount of $18,571 per eligible employee multiplied by the percentage of time devoted by that employee to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities during the year). While CRIC expenditures cannot be combined with other Québec provincial tax incentives for the same expense (such as the C3i investment and innovation credit), the CRIC stacks alongside the federal SR&ED ITC, and Revenu Québec typically processes properly documented CRIC refunds within 60 to 90 days. Claimants continue to report provincial R&D deductions on Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) in accordance with Revenu Québec publication IN-109-V (Tax Assistance for Scientific Research and Experimental Development).
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Bill C-15 Divergence

Enacted under Division 7 of Part 6 (sections 26.95 to 26.99) of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) per Information Circular IEG-1 and the Guide to Claiming the Innovation Employment Grant, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a fully refundable tax credit on up to $4,000,000 of annual eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 (yielding a maximum annual cash grant of $800,000). Claimed directly through the Alberta corporate tax system on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) alongside project listing Form AT4970 (entered on Line 129 of the AT1 return, with mandatory AT1 Net File in effect for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2024, and a filing deadline of 15 months after the AT1 filing due date), the IEG employs a two-tier incremental structure.

Under Part I of Schedule 29 (Line 110), a qualified corporation earns an 8 per cent base refundable credit on all eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to its maximum expenditure limit of $4,000,000 (prorated for short taxation years on Line 104 as days in the taxation year ÷ 365 and shared among associated corporations via the Schedule 29 allocation agreement). Under Part II of Schedule 29 (Lines 112 to 125), the corporation earns an additional 12 per cent incremental refundable credit—bringing the combined credit rate to 20 per cent—on the slice of current-year eligible Alberta R&D expenditures (up to the $4,000,000 cap) that exceeds the corporation's Base Amount. The Base Amount (Line 118 for non-associated corporations) is defined as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years (the average of Line 114 and Line 116). For example, an Alberta corporation with a two-year average baseline of $1,500,000 that incurs $3,000,000 of eligible Alberta R&D expenditures in the current taxation year receives 8 per cent on the first $1,500,000 ($120,000) plus 20 per cent (8 per cent base + 12 per cent incremental enhancement) on the $1,500,000 incremental spend above baseline ($300,000), resulting in a total refundable IEG of $420,000.

To focus support on small and medium-sized enterprises, the $4,000,000 Alberta IEG expenditure limit phases out linearly between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year federal taxable capital employed in Canada (taken from Line 690 of federal Schedule T2SCH33 and entered on Line 126 of Form AT29 for non-associated corporations, or Line 300 for associated groups), eliminating completely at $50,000,000:
Reduced expenditure limit = $4,000,000 × ($50,000,000 − prior-year taxable capital) ÷ $40,000,000
If property in respect of which an IEG was previously received is sold or converted to commercial use during the taxation year, IEG recapture is entered on Line 132 to reduce the net IEG on Line 134.

Crucially, corporate tax preparers must account for a major statutory divergence between federal Bill C-15 and the Alberta IEG regarding capital expenditures. For taxation years ending before December 16, 2024, Schedule 29 (Line 003 / Line 170) pulled the federal amount of qualified SR&ED expenditures from Line 559 of federal Form T661. However, because Alberta did not parallel the federal Bill C-15 restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures, Alberta TRA revised Schedule 29 to mandate that for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, claimants must use the federal amount of current SR&ED expenditures reported on Line 557 of federal Form T661, thereby excluding post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures from the Alberta IEG base. Furthermore, completing Form AT29 requires a two-step calculation: in Step 1, the claimant calculates the Alberta IEG on eligible Alberta current expenditures before deducting the IEG as provincial government assistance; in Step 2, that calculated IEG is entered on Line 513 of federal Form T661 to reduce the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool, ensuring that Line 170 of Form AT29 reconciles exactly with Line 557/559 of federal Form T661.
British Columbia, Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, corporations with a BC permanent establishment claim the BC SR&ED Tax Credit on T2 Schedule 425 (Form T666), earning a 10 per cent refundable credit for qualifying CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of annual eligible BC expenditures (phasing out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital) and a 10 per cent non-refundable credit for expenditures above the cap or incurred by non-CCPCs. In Manitoba, section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba) provides a 15 per cent R&D tax credit (reduced from 20 per cent for expenditures made after April 11, 2017) claimed on T2 Schedule 380 within one year after the corporation's filing due date. For in-house R&D in Manitoba, one-half (7.5 per cent) is refundable (entered on Line 613 of Schedule 5) and one-half (7.5 per cent) is non-refundable (entered on Line 606 of Schedule 5, with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward), whereas R&D conducted under an eligible contract with a qualifying research institute is 100 per cent refundable at the full 15 per cent rate. A corporation may renounce the Manitoba credit under subsection 7.3(7) up to one year after its filing due date, though for federal SR&ED purposes any renunciation must occur on or before six months after the corporation's taxation year-end. In Saskatchewan, corporations claim a 10 per cent R&D tax credit on T2 Schedule 403, where the expenditure limit for the refundable CCPC credit was recently doubled to $2,000,000 alongside the integration of post-December 15, 2024 capital and SUE expenditures. Finally, Nova Scotia (T2 Schedule 340), New Brunswick (T2 Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (T2 Schedule 301), and Yukon (T2 Schedule 442) each provide a 15 per cent fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure limit to all eligible corporations, and each updated its provincial schedule to incorporate capital and SUE expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024.
Ecosystem Interaction: Direct Innovation Grants and SR&ED Financing
Stacking and Grind Mechanics with Federal and Provincial Direct Grants

Canadian corporations frequently stack non-dilutive direct government grants and repayable contributions alongside SR&ED tax credits to fund capital-intensive technology roadmaps. Prominent direct funding programs operating across Canada in 2026 include the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative (RAII) delivered through Regional Development Agencies such as the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency (ACOA) (providing repayable contributions with a minimum ACOA commitment of $1,000,000) and PacifiCan in British Columbia (offering interest-free repayable contributions of $200,000 to $5,000,000 per project covering up to 50 per cent of eligible costs). In Western Canada, Alberta Innovates administers the AICE-Validate (up to $300,000) and AICE-Market Access ($300,000 to $600,000) grant streams, reimbursing up to 75 per cent of eligible project costs over 24 months with a minimum 25 per cent applicant cash or in-kind contribution. Nationally, CanExport Innovation reimburses up to 75 per cent of eligible costs (up to $37,500 per project and $100,000 per 12 months) to establish international R&D collaborations, while Ontario's Advanced Manufacturing and Innovation Competitiveness (AMIC) program provides interest-free loans for up to 4 years covering up to 15 per cent of eligible costs to $5,000,000 (with up to 30 per cent forgivable to $500,000) or direct grants of up to 15 per cent to $500,000 for small/rural businesses and $1,500,000 for strategic projects.

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, both non-repayable grants and government-backed forgivable or repayable contributions received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received on or before the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED constitute "government assistance" that reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditure base. However, because direct grants reduce the expenditure base rather than reducing the tax credit dollar-for-dollar, stacking a direct grant with the 35 per cent federal SR&ED ITC and provincial tax credits substantially increases net non-dilutive cash flow. Furthermore, when a claimant subsequently repays a repayable government contribution (such as an ACOA or PacifiCan RAII contribution or an AMIC loan) that previously reduced its SR&ED qualified expenditure pool, the repaid amount is added back to qualified expenditures on Line 560 of Form T661 (and the corresponding provincial schedule line, such as the Line 005 addition on Alberta Schedule 29) in the taxation year of repayment, generating newly earned SR&ED tax credits.
Private SR&ED Debt Financing

Because SR&ED claims are filed after the conclusion of the fiscal year and undergo CRA processing and potential technical or financial review before refund cheques are released—and because provincial disbursements such as the Alberta IEG are contingent upon CRA verification of the federal SR&ED claim—fast-growing enterprises frequently utilize specialized private SR&ED debt financing to eliminate working-capital lag. Specialized Canadian SR&ED lenders advance 70 per cent to 80 per cent of the expected federal and provincial refundable credit at interest rates typically ranging between 1 per cent and 2 per cent per month, with the credit facility retired directly when the CRA or Revenu Québec releases the tax refund.
Comprehensive Audit Defence and Strategic Recommendations

To maximize non-dilutive capital recovery while insulating claims against CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer audit adjustments under the post-Bill C-15 regime, corporate claimants and tax practitioners should execute five integrated compliance protocols.

First, engineering and scientific teams must institute contemporaneous hypothesis-driven documentation as R&D occurs during the taxation year. In accordance with Northwest Hydraulic, Zeuter Development, and Joel Theatrical Rigging, technical narratives on Form T661 must never frame commercial product features or custom engineering designs as the objective; instead, internal project tracking must contemporaneously record the specific technological uncertainty that standard practice could not resolve, the explicit scientific hypotheses formulated, the systematic test protocols and quantitative metrics observed, and the resulting advancement in underlying technological knowledge.

Second, enterprises planning high-value or technologically novel initiatives should leverage the CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process launched on April 1, 2026. By submitting a pre-claim application through My Business Account prior to commencing R&D or committing capital, corporations can secure a formal eligibility determination from the CRA within eight weeks, de-risking both internal capital allocation and private SR&ED debt financing.

Third, scale-up CCPCs and newly listed Canadian public corporations must optimize the Bill C-15 Expenditure Limit and Capital Restoration Rules. CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 due to venture equity or debt rounds should formally evaluate the new Bill C-15 election to calculate their expenditure limit phase-out using the three-year average gross revenue structure rather than taxable capital, preserving access to the full $6,000,000 expenditure cap and $2,100,000 cash refund ceiling. Concurrently, capital-intensive AI/ML, hardware, clean-tech, and biotech companies must track all depreciable equipment, GPU compute clusters, and shared-use equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, to claim restored federal and harmonizing provincial capital credits, while ensuring that post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures are excluded from Line 003 of Alberta AT1 Schedule 29 by referencing Line 557 of Form T661.

Fourth, corporations with establishments in Québec whose taxation years begin after March 25, 2025, must reconfigure their internal project-accounting systems for the Québec CRIC Regime. Because the CRIC replaces seven legacy credits and expands eligibility beyond pure R&D to encompass downstream pre-commercialization activities and capital equipment at a 30 per cent refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 (and 20 per cent thereafter), Québec claimants must track pre-commercialization salaries, CAPEX, and eligible research subcontracting separately from federal SR&ED while managing the $50,000 / $18,571-per-employee exclusion threshold.

Fifth, founder-led corporations must rigorously structure specified employee compensation prior to fiscal year-end. Because specified employees (shareholders owning 10 per cent or more of any class of shares) cannot claim bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, or prior-year unpaid wages, and are subject to the 75 per cent wage cap and the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base ceiling under Regulation 2900(7), founders performing hands-on R&D must be compensated through regular T4 base salary paid within the taxation year (or within 180 days of year-end) to preserve both their direct wage claim and the 55 per cent Prescribed Proxy Amount.
